reasons: The tool is small, has three subcommands, and one person will maintain it for years. argparse subparsers cover that fully. It is part of the standard library, so there is no dependency to upgrade, pin or have deprecated.

click and typer are both actively maintained. But typer is built on click, so a typer project inherits click's breaking changes as well as its own. I recall that click 8.2 (2025) changed some behavior and typer had to catch up. I did not verify this in this session.

argparse is still receiving improvements in current CPython. I recall that 3.14 (Oct 2025) added colored help and better error suggestions. The tool is on Python 3.11, which I recall is supported until about Oct 2027, so it would only get these when the interpreter is upgraded. argparse is not being phased out.

The strongest case against A is that argparse needs more boilerplate and has weaker ergonomics than typer's type-hint-driven approach. With only three subcommands that cost is small and happens once. A third-party dependency is a cost that recurs over years of maintenance.
risks: I did not run any web searches, so none of the release dates or version details above are verified. They come from memory: click 8.2 behavior changes, typer tracking click, argparse 3.14 features, and the 3.11 end-of-life date.
If the CLI grows to many nested subcommands, needs shell completion, or needs rich help output, click or typer would become more attractive.
The brief lists no files, so I could not check for existing conventions or dependencies in the repo.
would_change_if: The tool is expected to grow well beyond three subcommands, or the repo already depends on click or typer so that adding it costs nothing.
